questions.stem: Boreal (coniferous) forest is most extensive in:
options: the dry continental interiors of Australia and southern Africa
the subtropical west coasts of the continents between 20° and 30° latitude
the high latitudes of North America and Eurasia, roughly 50° to 70° N
the equatorial lowlands of the Amazon and Congo basins
questions.explanation: Boreal forest forms a broad belt across Canada, Alaska, Scandinavia and Russia, where winters are long and cold and summers short. The equatorial lowlands carry tropical rainforest, not coniferous forest.

questions.stem: Boreal forest is almost absent from the Southern Hemisphere. The main reason is that:
options: Southern Hemisphere winters are too mild for coniferous trees to survive
human clearing removed the boreal forests that once grew there
ice sheets cover all of the land south of 40° S
there is very little land at the latitudes where boreal forest grows
questions.explanation: Between about 50° and 70° S there is almost no land apart from the tip of South America and Antarctic islands, so the climate zone exists mostly over ocean. Clearing is not the explanation, as there was never an extensive boreal forest to clear.

questions.stem: Most of the world's hot deserts and other bare lands are found:
options: around the tropics, about 15° to 30° N and S, under subtropical high pressure
close to the Equator, where strongly rising air produces heavy convectional rain all year
along the polar circles, where winter darkness prevents plant growth
on the windward coasts of the mid-latitudes, facing the westerly winds
questions.explanation: Air descending in the subtropical high-pressure belts warms and dries, so the Sahara, Arabian, Kalahari and central Australian deserts lie near the tropics. Rising air at the Equator brings heavy rain and supports rainforest instead.

questions.stem: The two ice sheets that exist on Earth today are the:
options: Antarctic and Scandinavian ice sheets
Laurentide and Patagonian ice sheets
Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets
Greenland and Laurentide ice sheets
questions.explanation: Only Antarctica and Greenland hold ice masses large enough to be ice sheets today. The Laurentide and Scandinavian ice sheets covered North America and northern Europe during the last glacial period and have since melted.

questions.stem: Tropical savanna grassland is typically located between:
options: two mountain ranges in the mid-latitudes, where rain shadows form
tropical rainforest and hot desert, where a long dry season limits tree cover
boreal forest and tundra, where permafrost prevents the roots of trees from growing deep
temperate forest and ice sheets, where strong winds flatten the trees
questions.explanation: Savanna occupies the zone between the wet equatorial rainforests and the subtropical deserts, with a wet summer and a long dry season that favours grasses with scattered trees. Tundra borders the boreal forest, not the savanna.

questions.stem: A geographer notes that areas of alpine tundra closely match areas of high altitude on a map of a mountain range. This is an example of:
options: the movement of vegetation from lowland to highland areas
a change in land cover caused by human activity on the high slopes
a strong spatial association between altitude and vegetation
a weak spatial association between altitude and vegetation
questions.explanation: Spatial association is the degree to which two phenomena are similarly arranged over space, and here the two distributions match closely, so the association is strong. Temperature falls with altitude, so high slopes are too cold for trees.

questions.stem: A hypothetical region of 2 000 000 km² is 35% forest. A satellite survey shows that one-fifth of that forest has since been cleared. How much forest remains?
questions.explanation: The original forest is 35% of 2 000 000 km², which is 700 000 km². Removing one-fifth (140 000 km²) leaves 560 000 km²; 700 000 km² is the forest area before any clearing.

questions.stem: During the Last Glacial Maximum, about 20 000 years ago, global sea level was approximately:
options: 120 metres lower than today
120 metres higher than today
12 metres lower than today
the same as it is today
questions.explanation: So much water was locked in ice sheets on land that sea level fell by about 120 metres, exposing continental shelves. A rise rather than a fall would need less ice on land, which is the opposite of a glacial maximum.

questions.stem: As a result of lower sea level at the Last Glacial Maximum:
options: New Zealand was joined to eastern Australia across the Tasman Sea
Australia was joined to mainland Asia by continuous land through Indonesia
New Guinea, mainland Australia and Tasmania were joined as a single landmass
Australia was joined to Antarctica by a broad land bridge across the Southern Ocean
questions.explanation: The shallow Arafura Sea, Torres Strait and Bass Strait were exposed, joining the continent of Sahul. Deep water channels in eastern Indonesia remained, so Australia was never joined to Asia, and its separation from Antarctica happened tens of millions of years earlier.

questions.stem: At the Last Glacial Maximum, large ice sheets covered much of:
options: the Sahara and the Arabian Peninsula
South-east Asia and northern Australia
North America and northern Europe
South America and southern Africa
questions.explanation: The Laurentide ice sheet covered most of Canada and the northern United States, and the Scandinavian ice sheet covered northern Europe. The tropics and subtropics remained ice-free apart from high mountains.

questions.stem: Compared with today, tropical rainforest at the Last Glacial Maximum was:
options: more extensive, because the cooler climate brought heavier rainfall
unchanged, because the tropics were unaffected by the glacial period
absent altogether, because ice sheets reached the Equator
less extensive, because the global climate was cooler and drier
questions.explanation: A colder, drier glacial climate shrank rainforests into smaller refuges, with grassland and dry woodland expanding around them. The tropics did change, but ice never reached the Equator except on the highest mountains.

questions.stem: During the Holocene Climatic Optimum, about 8000 years ago, much of the Sahara:
options: was wetter than today, with grasslands, lakes and wetlands where there is now desert
was covered by an ice cap that spread south from the Atlas Mountains
was even drier than today, with sand seas extending into southern Europe
had the same bare land cover that it has today
questions.explanation: Stronger monsoon rains in this period produced a 'green Sahara', with grasslands, lakes and wetlands across land that is now desert. Ice caps did not form there, and the region was wetter, not drier, than at present.

questions.stem: A student compares land cover maps of the Northern Hemisphere for 20 000 years ago and 8000 years ago. Which change should the student identify?
options: Tundra had spread south across Europe into areas that had been forest 20 000 years earlier
The ice sheets had grown to their greatest extent over North America and Europe
Sea level had fallen, exposing new land bridges between the continents
The ice sheets had largely melted and forest had spread north into former tundra
questions.explanation: Between the Last Glacial Maximum and the Holocene Climatic Optimum the climate warmed, the ice sheets largely melted and the treeline moved north into former tundra. Sea level rose over this period as meltwater returned to the oceans, so land bridges were flooded rather than exposed.

questions.stem: The cycles of glacial and interglacial periods over the past million years are mainly triggered by:
options: large meteorite impacts every few thousand years
regular changes in Earth's orbit and the tilt of its axis
the burning of fossil fuels since the Industrial Revolution
the clearing of forests by early farming societies
questions.explanation: Milankovitch cycles in Earth's orbit, tilt and wobble change how much sunlight reaches high northern latitudes in summer, which paces glacial cycles. Fossil fuel burning is the main cause of present warming, but it began only a few centuries ago.

questions.stem: In one year a glacier gains 2.4 million tonnes of ice in its accumulation zone and loses 3.1 million tonnes in its ablation zone. Which statement is correct?
options: It has a negative mass balance of 5.5 million tonnes, so it will disappear within a year
Its mass balance cannot be calculated without knowing its speed of flow
It has a negative mass balance of 0.7 million tonnes, so it will thin or retreat
It has a positive mass balance of 0.7 million tonnes, so its snout will advance
questions.explanation: Mass balance is gains minus losses: 2.4 − 3.1 = −0.7 million tonnes, so the glacier is shrinking. Adding the two figures to get 5.5 confuses a balance with a total.

questions.stem: The snout of a valley glacier has retreated 300 m up its valley over 20 years. Which statement about the glacier is correct?
options: Its ice is still flowing downhill, but melting at the snout exceeds the ice supplied from above
Its ice has reversed direction and is now flowing back up the valley towards its source
Its accumulation zone must be growing, which is pulling the snout up the valley
Its ice has stopped moving, because a retreating glacier no longer flows at all
questions.explanation: Glacier ice always flows downhill under gravity; a retreating snout means ablation at the front is greater than the supply of ice from upstream. The ice does not flow backwards, and a growing accumulation zone would push the snout forward, not pull it back.

questions.stem: Farmers who clear tropical rainforest for crops often find that yields fall within a few years. The main reason is that:
options: most nutrients were held in the vegetation, and the exposed soil is quickly leached by heavy rain
the soil becomes waterlogged once the canopy no longer intercepts the rain
the cleared land becomes too cold for crops without the shelter of the trees
the ash from burning the forest makes the soil too acidic for any crop
questions.explanation: In rainforests, nutrients cycle rapidly through living plants and leaf litter, so the soils themselves are poor; once the forest is removed, heavy rain leaches what remains. Ash from burning actually adds some nutrients briefly, which is why yields are highest in the first year or two.

questions.stem: The loss of snow and ice cover can speed up warming in polar and mountain regions because:
options: exposed rock reflects more sunlight onto the remaining ice, melting it from above
meltwater forms clouds that trap heat and stop any further snowfall
darker exposed land and water absorb more solar radiation than reflective ice
melting ice releases large amounts of carbon dioxide trapped in the ice itself
questions.explanation: Ice and snow have a high albedo and reflect most incoming sunlight; when they melt, darker surfaces absorb more energy, causing more warming and more melting. This is a positive feedback, and exposed rock has a lower albedo than ice, not a higher one.

questions.stem: Most deforestation in the world today is taking place in:
options: subtropical deserts such as the Sahara and the Arabian Peninsula
tropical regions such as the Amazon, the Congo Basin and South-east Asia
boreal regions such as Canada, Scandinavia and Siberia, where logging is most intense
temperate regions such as western and central Europe
questions.explanation: Net forest loss is concentrated in the tropics, where forest is cleared for pasture, crops, plantations and mining. Forest area in much of Europe is stable or increasing.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the global distribution of glacier retreat?
options: It is occurring only in the Southern Hemisphere, where most of the world's glaciers are found
It is occurring only on mountains near the Equator, where temperatures are highest
It is occurring in most glaciated mountain regions, including the Alps, the Himalaya and the Andes
It is occurring only in polar regions, while mountain glaciers at lower latitudes are stable or growing
questions.explanation: Retreat is widespread on every continent that has glaciers, from Alaska and the Alps to the Himalaya, the Andes and New Zealand. It is not confined to one latitude or one hemisphere.

questions.stem: A hypothetical table gives tree cover lost over a decade as a percentage of each region's forest: W 0.2%, X 4.5%, Y 3.8%, Z 0.1%. W and Z are temperate; X and Y are tropical. Which conclusion is supported?
options: Region Y lost a higher percentage of its forest than Region X
The tropical regions lost a far higher percentage of their forest than the temperate regions
The temperate regions lost a higher percentage of their forest than the tropical regions
All four regions lost a broadly similar percentage of their forest cover over the decade
questions.explanation: Both tropical regions lost close to 4–5% of their forest, against 0.1–0.2% in the temperate regions. Region Y's 3.8% is lower than Region X's 4.5%, so that statement reverses the data.

questions.stem: Using the same table of percentage forest loss, a student concludes that Region X lost more hectares of forest than any other region. Why is this conclusion not supported?
options: Percentages are always smaller than areas, so the hectares lost must be about the same in each of the four regions
Region X lost the highest percentage, so it must have lost the fewest hectares of all
The table gives percentages, so without each region's forest area the hectares lost cannot be compared
Region Y must have lost more hectares, because tropical regions always contain the most forest
questions.explanation: A percentage describes loss relative to each region's own forest, so a large forest losing 3.8% could lose more hectares than a small forest losing 4.5%. The conclusion needs the forest area of each region before it can be tested.

questions.stem: The main cause of the accelerated melting of glaciers and ice sheets since the late 1800s is:
options: heat released by volcanic eruptions beneath the ice
a long-term increase in snowfall and cloud cover over the polar regions
warming from greenhouse gases released mainly by burning fossil fuels
a change in Earth's orbit that has brought it closer to the Sun
questions.explanation: The enhanced greenhouse effect, driven by carbon dioxide from fossil fuels and land clearing, has raised global temperatures and increased melting. Orbital changes act over tens of thousands of years and are far too slow to explain change over a century.

questions.stem: Which is a natural cause of increased melting on the surface of a glacier?
options: Dark ash from a volcanic eruption settling on the ice
Soot from diesel engines and coal burning settling on the ice
Dust from a nearby open-cut mine settling on the ice
Warming caused by greenhouse gases from power stations
questions.explanation: Volcanic ash lowers the albedo of the ice so it absorbs more sunlight, and volcanic eruptions are a natural process. Soot, mine dust and greenhouse warming all lower albedo or raise temperature too, but they come from human activity.

questions.stem: Much of the recent ice loss from West Antarctica is linked to warmer ocean water. The process involved is that:
options: warm air above the ocean melts the surface of the interior ice sheet every summer
warm water evaporates and falls as rain over the ice sheet, washing the ice away
warm water freezes onto the base of the ice shelves, making them heavy enough to sink
warm water melts floating ice shelves from below, so the glaciers they hold back flow faster
questions.explanation: Ice shelves buttress the glaciers behind them; when warm ocean water thins them from below, the land ice flows into the sea more quickly. Air temperatures over the high interior remain well below freezing, so surface melting there is not the main cause.

questions.stem: The leading direct cause of deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon has been clearing for:
options: wheat farms
cattle pasture
oil palm plantations
urban housing
questions.explanation: Most cleared land in the Brazilian Amazon has been converted to pasture for beef cattle, with soy and other crops also important. Oil palm is the major driver in Indonesia and Malaysia, not Brazil.

questions.stem: In Indonesia and Malaysia, a major cause of the clearing of lowland rainforest and peat swamp forest has been:
options: the growth of tundra caused by a cooling climate
the expansion of oil palm plantations
the expansion of cattle ranching for beef exports
the spread of wheat farming into the lowlands
questions.explanation: Large areas of lowland and peat swamp forest in Sumatra and Borneo have been converted to oil palm and pulpwood plantations. Cattle ranching is the main driver in the Amazon rather than South-east Asia.

questions.stem: A satellite image of part of the Amazon shows cleared land in a 'fishbone' pattern along a highway and the side roads branching from it. What does this pattern show?
options: Clearing caused by natural fires that spread along dry ridges and avoid the roads
Clearing caused by rivers changing course and flooding the forest beside them
A strong spatial association between roads and clearing, because roads give settlers access
A weak spatial association between roads and clearing, because the clearing is random
questions.explanation: The cleared strips line the highway and its side roads, so the two distributions closely match: road building opens the forest to settlers, loggers and ranchers. A random or weak pattern would not follow the roads so closely.

questions.stem: Large-scale clearing of the Amazon may reduce rainfall in regions downwind because:
options: cleared land reflects less sunlight, so the air above it becomes too cool to rise
the carbon dioxide released by burning blocks rain from forming in clouds
bare soil releases moisture into the air faster than forest does
less evapotranspiration means less moisture is recycled into the atmosphere
questions.explanation: Rainforest trees return large amounts of water to the air through evapotranspiration, and winds carry this moisture to other regions where it falls as rain. Bare or grassed land returns much less, and cleared land reflects more sunlight, not less.

questions.stem: Records for a glacier-fed river in the Andes show dry-season flow rising for several decades as the glacier shrank, then beginning to fall. The best explanation is that:
options: faster melting first released more stored ice, but the shrinking glacier then had less ice left to melt
rainfall must have risen and then fallen, because glaciers have no real effect on the dry-season flow of rivers
the glacier began to grow again in the later decades, storing more water as ice
upstream dams increased river flow at first, then released no water at all
questions.explanation: This pattern is called 'peak water': melting a glacier faster increases runoff for a time, but as the ice store shrinks, meltwater declines. Glaciers are a major source of dry-season flow in the Andes, so they cannot be ignored.

questions.stem: As a Himalayan glacier retreats, a lake forms behind the loose moraine left at its former snout. The main hazard this creates for villages downstream is:
options: a long drought caused by the lake trapping all of the river's water
an earthquake triggered by the weight of the water in the lake
a glacial lake outburst flood if the moraine dam fails
a tsunami caused by the lake water freezing suddenly in winter
questions.explanation: Moraine dams are made of unconsolidated debris and can fail suddenly, releasing the lake as a destructive flood. The lake overflows into the river as it fills, so it does not trap all the river's water.

questions.stem: Floating ice already displaces its own weight of sea water. Using this idea, which melting would directly raise global sea level?
options: An Antarctic ice shelf, which floats on the ocean
Icebergs already floating in the Southern Ocean
The Greenland ice sheet, which rests on land
Arctic sea ice, which floats on the ocean
questions.explanation: Ice resting on land adds new water to the ocean when it melts or flows into the sea, so it raises sea level. Sea ice, ice shelves and icebergs are already floating, so their melting adds almost nothing directly.

questions.stem: Which is an economic benefit of forest clearing for a country such as Brazil?
options: Increased tourism from visitors who come to see intact forest
Higher payments for keeping carbon stored in the forest
Export income from beef and soy produced on cleared land
Greater rainfall for the hydroelectric dams downwind of the clearing
questions.explanation: Cleared land produces beef and soy that earn export income and create jobs, which is why clearing continues despite its costs. Clearing reduces carbon storage, so it loses carbon payments rather than earning them.

questions.stem: Which impact of deforestation in the Amazon is best classified as social?
options: Conflict over land between Indigenous communities and loggers, ranchers and miners
Soil erosion and the silting of rivers after the forest cover is removed
Income from timber exports earned by logging companies
Loss of habitat for species found nowhere else on Earth
questions.explanation: Social impacts concern people's lives, communities and wellbeing, such as conflict, displacement and loss of traditional livelihoods. Soil erosion and habitat loss are environmental impacts, and timber export income is economic.

questions.stem: Satellite vegetation indices such as NDVI can identify healthy forest because healthy leaves:
options: reflect radio waves that satellites receive from the ground
strongly reflect near-infrared light and absorb red light
strongly absorb near-infrared light and reflect red light
give off heat that satellites detect as visible green light
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll absorbs red light for photosynthesis, while healthy leaf structure reflects near-infrared strongly, so the contrast between the two bands indicates vegetation health. Reversing the two bands describes bare or stressed surfaces, not healthy forest.

questions.stem: Brazil's DETER system, run by its national space research institute, uses satellite data to:
options: count the cattle grazing on each property in the Amazon each year for tax purposes
send near-real-time alerts of new clearing so that enforcement agencies can act
plant new trees automatically in areas where clearing has been detected
measure the thickness of glacier ice in the Andes each month
questions.explanation: DETER detects new clearing from frequent satellite images and passes alerts to environmental enforcement officers, while the separate PRODES system measures annual clearing. Satellites monitor change; they do not replant forest.

questions.stem: Why do some tropical forest-monitoring programs add satellite radar images to optical satellite images?
options: Radar can count the individual species of trees in the canopy, which optical images cannot do
Radar images are taken from aircraft, so they cover larger areas than any satellite can
Radar can image the ground through the cloud that often hides tropical forests from optical sensors
Radar images are in natural colour, so they are easier for the public to understand than optical images
questions.explanation: Tropical forests are frequently under cloud, which blocks optical sensors; radar penetrates cloud and works at night, giving more regular coverage. Radar does not produce natural-colour images or identify individual species.

questions.stem: The Paris Agreement, a global response to climate change and melting ice, aims to:
options: hold warming to well below 2 °C above pre-industrial levels and pursue a limit of 1.5 °C
stop all fossil fuel use worldwide within five years of the agreement being signed in Paris
rebuild lost glaciers by producing artificial snow on mountain ranges
require only developed countries to report their greenhouse gas emissions
questions.explanation: Under the Paris Agreement each country sets nationally determined contributions to cut emissions towards the shared temperature goals. It does not set a five-year deadline for ending fossil fuel use, and all parties, not only developed countries, report on their emissions.

questions.stem: REDD+ is a global response to deforestation that works by:
options: banning all international trade in timber and other forest products
requiring developed countries to plant one tree for every tree cleared in the tropics
buying tropical forests outright and making them the property of the United Nations
paying developing countries for verified reductions in emissions from forest loss and degradation
questions.explanation: REDD+ (reducing emissions from deforestation and forest degradation) gives results-based payments to countries that can show, through monitoring, that they have reduced forest loss. It does not ban timber trade or transfer ownership of forests.

questions.stem: In Switzerland, parts of the Rhône Glacier near a tourist ice grotto are covered with white fleece each summer to slow melting. Which is the best evaluation of this response?
options: It is highly effective, because covering a small area stops the whole glacier from retreating
It is ineffective, because white fleece absorbs more sunlight than the glacier's ice
It addresses the main cause of melting, because the fleece removes greenhouse gases from the air
It reduces melting where applied but is too costly and small-scale to protect glaciers generally
questions.explanation: The fleece reflects sunlight and insulates the ice, so melting slows under the covers, protecting a tourist attraction. However, it covers only a tiny fraction of the glacier and does nothing about the warming that causes the retreat.

questions.stem: Brazil's Forest Code responds to deforestation at the national scale by requiring rural landholders in forested areas of the Amazon to:
options: sell their land to the government once forest cover falls below half
clear no more than one hectare in total over their lifetime
keep 80% of their property under native vegetation as a legal reserve
replant every hectare they clear with native trees within twelve months
questions.explanation: The Forest Code sets a legal reserve of 80% of each property in forested parts of the Legal Amazon, with lower proportions in other biomes. Its effectiveness depends heavily on monitoring and enforcement.

questions.stem: The Amazon Soy Moratorium, begun in 2006, is a response in which:
options: Brazil's government banned the growing of soy anywhere in the country
farmers agreed to plant soy beneath the rainforest canopy instead of clearing it
importing countries agreed to pay a higher price for soy grown in the Amazon
major soy traders agreed not to buy soy grown on Amazon land cleared after a cut-off date
questions.explanation: The moratorium was an agreement by traders, supported by environmental groups and monitored with satellite imagery, to refuse soy from newly cleared Amazon land. It did not ban soy farming, which continues on land cleared earlier and in other regions.

questions.stem: In a hypothetical country, annual deforestation fell from 20 000 km² to 5 000 km² in the eight years after a satellite monitoring and enforcement program began. Which evaluation is best?
options: The program failed, because some forest was still being cleared at the end of the period
The 75% fall is consistent with success, but other factors such as falling beef prices must be checked
The 75% fall proves the program alone caused the decline, so no further evidence is needed
The fall was 300%, which shows the program was more effective than any other response
questions.explanation: The fall is 15 000 out of 20 000 km², or 75%, which supports the program's effectiveness, but a careful evaluation considers other causes such as commodity prices or economic conditions. Dividing 15 000 by 5 000 gives the 300% error.
